recipe.history:
Béarnaise sauce is a child of the classical French kitchen and one of the great achievements of nineteenth-century culinary systematization. It is generally attributed to the chef Collinet, who is said to have created it around 1837 at a restaurant called Le Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, just outside Paris, though like most origin stories for classic sauces, this one is disputed and likely simplified. What is certain is that béarnaise belongs to the family of warm emulsified butter sauces derived from hollandaise, differing in its use of a reduction base — a concentrated infusion of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallots, and fresh tarragon — which is incorporated into the egg yolk emulsion before the butter is mounted. The result is a sauce of extraordinary richness cut through with a herbaceous, anise-adjacent sharpness that makes it the definitive companion to beef. The region of Béarn in southwestern France, for which the sauce is nominally named, had no particular role in its invention, but the name stuck and the sauce became one of the pillars of escoffier-era haute cuisine.

Béarnaise made its way into American restaurant culture through the fine dining establishments of the mid-twentieth century, where it appeared alongside filet mignon and prime rib on white-tablecloth menus from New York to San Francisco. Julia Child's television work in the 1960s and 1970s demystified the classical French repertoire for home cooks and made béarnaise achievable outside of professional kitchens, though it retained its reputation as a technically demanding sauce prone to breaking if not treated with care. The sauce's migration to the burger world was a natural consequence of the premium burger movement — once chefs began sourcing dry-aged beef and using cast-iron technique, the logical pairing with the sauce that had always been beef's finest companion became inevitable.

The first béarnaise I made from scratch took me three attempts over a single afternoon. The first broke when I added the butter too quickly; the second scrambled when the heat climbed too high; the third held — and held beautifully, a thick, pale gold, glossy emulsion that smelled like tarragon and butter and shallots and summer. I ate it with a spoon before anything else was ready. There is something almost alchemical about a sauce that should not work — raw egg yolk, cold butter, heat, acid — and does, and becomes this thing that is silkier and more complex than any of its parts suggest. I have never once thought, while making béarnaise, that it wasn't worth the effort. It is always worth the effort.

Béarnaise sauce and a medium-rare beef patty are not merely compatible — they are, in some fundamental sense, made for each other. The sauce was designed for beef cooked to the point where the interior is warm, pink, yielding, and full of juice; its fat content and acidity are calibrated to enrich and cut through exactly that texture. A well-done patty produces none of the meat juices that mingle with the sauce on the plate, none of the tender interior that takes on the béarnaise and carries it through each bite. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — the patty is medium rare, its fibers relaxed, its fat distributed evenly, its surface seared to a crackling crust. The béarnaise pools in every crevice and the two become briefly, beautifully inseparable.
ingredients: 8 oz (225g) ground beef, 80/20 chuck blend — ideally dry-aged if available
2 tbsp white wine vinegar or tarragon vinegar
1 tbsp fresh tarragon leaves, roughly chopped (for reduction)
1 tbsp fresh tarragon leaves, finely chopped (for finishing)
1 tbsp fresh chervil or flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Squeeze of lemon juice to taste
instructions: 1. Clarify the butter: melt the butter in a small saucepan over low heat until the milk solids separate and settle to the bottom. Skim the foam from the top and carefully pour the golden clarified butter into a small bowl, leaving the milky solids behind. Keep warm.

2. Make the béarnaise reduction: combine white wine, white wine vinegar, minced shallots, and the first tablespoon of tarragon in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce until only about 1 tablespoon of liquid remains. Strain through a fine mesh sieve, pressing on the solids. Allow to cool to room temperature.
3. Set up a double boiler: bring a small saucepan of water to a gentle simmer. Place a heatproof bowl over the saucepan — the bottom of the bowl must not touch the water.

4. Combine egg yolks, the cooled reduction, and 1 teaspoon of cold water in the double boiler bowl. Whisk vigorously and continuously over the simmering water until the mixture thickens, becomes pale, and triples in volume — about 3 to 5 minutes. It should hold a ribbon when the whisk is lifted. Do not let the bowl overheat.

5. Remove the bowl from the heat. Begin adding the warm clarified butter one drop at a time while whisking constantly, then in a very slow, thin stream as the emulsion establishes itself. Continue until all butter is incorporated and the sauce is thick and glossy.

6. Season with salt, white pepper, and a squeeze of lemon juice. Fold in the remaining chopped fresh tarragon and chervil or parsley. Keep warm in the double boiler over very low heat, whisking occasionally. If the sauce thickens too much, whisk in a few drops of warm water.
7. Cook the bacon in a skillet over medium heat until crispy, 4 to 5 minutes per side. Drain on paper towels.

8. Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Form gently into a single patty about 4 inches in diameter and 3/4-inch thick. Press a dimple in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper.
9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat.
10. Place the patty in the pan and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to form a deep crust.
11. Flip once. Lay Gruyère slices on top immediately. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes.
12. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3 minutes.
13. Melt butter in a separate pan over medium heat. Toast the brioche bun cut-side down until golden, 1 to 2 minutes.
14. Spread Dijon mustard on the bottom bun. Place watercress and tomato slices on the bottom bun.
15. Add the rested medium-rare patty with melted Gruyère, then lay the bacon strips over the cheese.
16. Spoon a generous amount of béarnaise sauce directly over the patty and bacon, allowing it to drape over the sides.
17. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun.
18. Serve immediately with additional béarnaise sauce on the side for dipping.
